correctness.rationale: The proof covers \(b=0\), every power-of-two candidate, and every possible odd prime factor. In the branch \(p\equiv1\pmod3\), LTE gives exact \(3\)-adic valuation one for \(p^{2t}+p^t+1\), which is greater than \(3\), forcing a forbidden non-\(3\) prime factor. All quantifiers are unrestricted, and the finite checker is explicitly non-probative.

evidence: The prior implication \(\Sigma^{*}(N)\ge2\) when \(3\mid N\) supplies only the lower half of the equality.

originality.rationale: The foundational full text was inspected at the definition/table, all theorem statements, the odd-divisor-sum lemma, and the final theorem section. It records \(\Sigma^{*}(3)=\Sigma^{*}(9)=\Sigma^{*}(27)=2\) and related bounds but not the all-exponent identity or the classification \(\sigma(n)=3^b\). OEIS A319068 and the later unitary analogue do not imply the claim. Semantic searches returned only different divisor-sum, harmonic, and unitary problems.
residual_risks: An older or poorly indexed note on inverse values of the ordinary divisor-sum function could contain the elementary classification \(\sigma(n)=3^b\).
The exact publication day for the 2005 source is supplied by bibliographic metadata rather than printed in the scanned paper.

value.rationale: This closes a natural prime-power ray of the sum-of-divisors maximum function that the foundational paper samples at \(3\), \(9\), and \(27\) but does not settle uniformly. The equivalent inverse-image theorem is a complete structural classification, not a finite computation or arbitrary slice, and it explains why the ternary ray is constant.
